question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, why had soap-making tallow become less important to British tallow melters?
reference_answer: Rising demand for edible fat led melters to select and render much rough fat separately for sale to margarine makers, leaving tallow melted for soap-making as a secondary product.
required_key_points: Much rough fat was sold for margarine-making.
supporting_passage:
Owing to the increasing
demand for edible fat, much of the rough fat is carefully selected,
rendered separately, and the product sold for margarine-making.
Consequently the melted tallow for soap-making is of secondary
importance to the tallow melter.

section: VARIOUS NEW FATS AND OILS SUGGESTED FOR SOAP-MAKING.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, which investigators do the authors associate, in chronological order, with research on Niam fat?
reference_answer: Lewkowitsch examined Niam fat first; Edie later published an analysis of it.
supporting_passage:
The fat, as prepared by natives, has been
examined by Lewkowitsch, and more recently Edie has published the
results of an analysis.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what precise procedure did the authors describe for grading barrels of rosin?
reference_answer: A sample from the top of every barrel was cut into uniformly sized cubes 7/8 of an inch across; the shade of a cube determined the rosin’s grade and value.
required_key_points: Samples were taken from the top of every barrel.
Samples were cut into uniform 7/8 of an inch cubes.
The shade of colour of each cube determined its grade and value.
supporting_passage:
It is graded by samples taken out of the
top of every barrel, and cut into 7/8 of an inch cubes, which must be
uniform in size--the shade of colour of the cube determines its grade
and value.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, how do the authors describe removing excess colour from the mucilage used to manufacture soapstock?
reference_answer: They boil the mucilage with water, grain it well with salt, and repeat the treatment several times until the product no longer has excess colour.
required_key_points: Repeat the treatment several times until free from excess colour.
supporting_passage:
The
colouring matter is removed by boiling the mucilage with water and
graining well with salt; this treatment is repeated several times until
the product is free from excess of colour, when it is converted into
soap and a nigre settled out from it.

section: LESS-KNOWN OILS AND FATS OF LIMITED USE.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, how was Tangawang fat shaped for export to Europe as Borneo Tallow?
reference_answer: It was moulded using bamboo canes into rolls about 3 inches thick.
required_key_points: Moulded by means of bamboo canes.
Formed into rolls about 3 inches thick.
supporting_passage:
_Borneo Tallow._--The kernels of several species of _Hopea_ (or
_Dipterocarpus_), which flourish in the Malayan Archipelago, yield a fat
known locally as Tangawang fat. This fat is moulded (by means of bamboo
canes) into the form of rolls about 3 inches thick, and exported to
Europe as Borneo Tallow.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, which two constituents, with their percentages, did the authors report alongside carbonate of soda in 48 deg. soda ash?
reference_answer: It often contained 4 per cent. caustic soda (sodium hydrate) and 10 per cent. salt (sodium chloride).
supporting_passage:
_Soda ash_, 48 deg., sometimes called "caustic soda ash," often contains
besides carbonate of soda, 4 per cent. caustic soda (sodium hydrate),
and 10 per cent. salt (sodium chloride), together with water and
impurities.
